program: Travel English -- Europe Without a Translator
hub_subtitle: Travel English for the airport, the check-in counter, the hotel and passport control — so that Europe needs no translator

lesson.menu_title: Talking About People -- The Ones You Travel With
lesson.menu_desc: A breakfast table in Sorrento, a stranger who asks "are you traveling alone?" -- and four sentences that turn a polite answer into a real conversation. The husband who speaks no English stops being the silent man at the table and becomes a person the others have met. The grammar: comparing two people -- quieter than me, more patient than me, better English than I do, not as talkative as his brother. New words for people: outgoing, shy, patient, easygoing, generous, stubborn, talkative, hardworking, to get along with, to take after -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- Talking About People
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosângela | Lesson 17 -- Talking About People
lesson.grammar_point: comparative adjectives for people (-er than / more ... than / irregular better and worse / (not) as ... as)

listenings.text: My name is Antonio, and for eighteen years I have carried coffee to the same breakfast room in Sorrento, so believe me when I tell you: I know people. Every morning I watch the tables, and I can tell you who is who before anybody says good morning. There is always one person who is more talkative than everybody else, who says good morning to the whole room, and there is always somebody quieter, behind the newspaper, who only wants the coffee. Neither one is better than the other. But here is the thing I have learned in eighteen years. The couples who enjoy the trip most are almost never the ones with the best English. They are the ones who talk about their people. A woman from Brazil sat at table nine last summer, with her husband. He did not speak one word of English, not one, and he was much shyer than she was. But she talked. She told me her husband was more easygoing than her, that he was never in a hurry, that he was happy on the balcony with the sun. She told me her son was more fluent than the whole family together, and that he was twenty-four now, and traveling with his friends. In ten minutes I knew her family better than I know some of my neighbors, and her English was still growing. So do not wait until your English is perfect to talk about the people you love. Tell me who your husband is. Tell me who is the patient one, and who is the stubborn one. That is not grammar. That is friendship, and it starts at breakfast.

I am Marina, I am seventy-one, and I travel with a husband who does not speak English. For a long time, that was the loneliest part of my trips. Somebody would smile at us in a hotel, or on a boat, and ask a friendly question, and I would answer with four words: I am Marina, from Brazil. And then the conversation would stop, because I had nothing else. I knew the words for the airport and the words for the hotel, but I had no words for the people I love, and so my husband would sit next to me like a piece of luggage, and the other people never met him. And then, on a bus in Portugal, a woman asked me about him. And instead of stopping at four words, I tried. I said: he is quieter than me, he is not as brave as me with languages, but he is more patient than anybody, and he is the most generous man I know. Three sentences. My English was not better that day than the day before, but everything changed. The woman laughed and said her husband was exactly the same, and we talked for an hour, and at the end she came to meet him. Here is what nobody tells you. To make a friend in another country, you do not need perfect grammar. You need to be able to say who your people are: who is the talkative one, who is shy, who is easygoing, who never changes his mind. Learn those five or six words, and you stop traveling as a tourist. You start traveling as a person with a family.

structure.title: Four ways to put two people side by side
cards: Quiet, calm, young, old, tall: just add -er, and then than. "He's quieter than me." "My brother is younger than me." If the adjective ends in -y, the y becomes -ier: happy becomes happier, easy becomes easier, funny becomes funnier.

Patient, outgoing, generous, easygoing, talkative, hardworking: these are too long for -er, so more goes in front. "He's more patient than me." "She's more generous than anybody." Never both together: more quieter and more patienter do not exist.
Good and bad go their own way
Good becomes better, and bad becomes worse. "My son speaks better English than I do." "The second hotel was worse than the first one." Never gooder, never more good, never more better.

Use as ... as when two people are equal: "He's as old as my brother." Use not as ... as to say somebody has less, gently: "He isn't as brave as me with English." The word as appears twice, on both sides of the adjective -- never as brave than.

items.situation: A guest at the next table asks: "Are you traveling alone?" Answer, and say why your husband is not talking.
tips: No, I'm here with my husband. He doesn't speak English, so I do the talking for both of us.
I'm with my husband. He's on the balcony -- he understands a little, but he doesn't speak.

items.situation: The same guest asks what your husband is like. Say one thing, with a comparison.
tips: He's quieter than me, but he's much more easygoing.
He's more patient than I am. Three hours in an airport, and he never complains.

items.situation: They ask about your son. Say how old he is and compare his English with yours.
tips: He's twenty-four, and he speaks better English than I do.
My son is fluent -- his English is much better than mine, and he's very hardworking.

items.situation: They ask if your son is like you or like his father.
tips: He takes after me. He's as talkative as I am.
He takes after me -- he talks to everybody, like his mother.

items.situation: Say something kind about a friend who is very generous.
tips: She's more generous than anybody I know.
My friend is the most generous person at any table -- she always pays first.

items.situation: Say, gently, that your husband is less brave than you with English.
tips: He isn't as brave as me with English.
He's not as confident as I am in English, but he understands more than he says.

items.situation: The guest tells you their brother never changes his mind. Agree, and say who is like that in your family.
tips: My brother is the same -- he's very stubborn!
Mine too. My husband is a little stubborn: the map is wrong, never him.

items.situation: The conversation is ending, and you want it to continue. Ask them about their family.
tips: And you? Do you travel with your family?
What about you? Who do you usually travel with?
